messages.subject: Help parameterizing a constrained simplex?
parts:
Hi,

Still working on my dissertation model, and I have a question about how best to parameterize the prior for the epidemiological "contact matrix." (It runs now, but it's not at all elegant, and I'm hoping there are nice solutions to do this.)

This type of matrix matrix has entries c(a,b) that are the number of times an individual in group a is in contact with an individual in group b. It is constrained by the fact that contact is symmetric - though groups sizes are not equal. This means c(b,a) = c(a,b)*size(a)/size(b).

As an additional concern, I had earlier changed the contact matrix to be a simplex that was then multiplied by a fixed value, because allowing the total number of contacts to vary was interacting with the estimated spread variable. (More viral flu with fewer contacts looks exactly like a less viral flu with more contacts.) I found (unsurprisingly) that Stan was arriving at implausible contact matrix simplex posteriors. Using a static prior contact matrix was much faster than having Stan estimate the values, but I'd prefer to allow it to estimate the values based on the provided values as priors.

So, I am attempting to figure out how I can parameterize the model to include a simplex that obeys a constraint. To do this, I use a simplex for the upper triangular part of the matrix, then enforce the constraint on the other half, and then normalize the entire thing all together.

The relevant parts of my attempt (excluding the actual infectious disease model parts,) which seems to work but is very kludge-y:


Data:
  real<lower=0> contact_matrix[groups,groups]; // These are unknown, but depend on the group types. This (approximate) matrix here will be used in the prior.

Transformed Data:
  real Upper_Contact_Matrix[groups*(groups+1)/2];
{
int upper_counter;
upper_counter <- 1;
Contact_Matrix_Normalizer <- 0.0;
for (i in 1:groups) {
for (j in 1:groups) {
                if (i<=j){
Upper_Contact_Matrix[upper_counter]<-contact_matrix[i,j];
upper_counter <- upper_counter + 1;
}
Contact_Matrix_Normalizer <- Contact_Matrix_Normalizer + contact_matrix[i,j]; //This is based on the total
}
}
}

Parameters:
  simplex[groups*(groups+1)/2] contact_matrix_vector; //Upper triangular portion only.

Transformed Parameters:
  real upper_simplex_pct; //The percentage of the total in the upper simplex - used for normalizing later.
  real<lower=0> Lower_Triangular_Simplex[groups*(groups-1)/2];

  {
  real contact_matrix_temp[groups,groups];
  int upper_counter;
  int lower_counter;
  upper_counter <- 1;
  lower_counter <- 1;
  for (i in 1:groups) {
    for (j in 1:groups) {
      real inverse_value;
 inverse_value <- (-1); //If my logic is bad, this will violate constraints later.
      if (i>j) {
   contact_matrix_temp[i,j] <- contact_matrix_temp[j,i]*pop_sizes[j]/pop_sizes[i]; //This creates the contact matrix identity.
   Lower_Triangular_Simplex[lower_counter] <- contact_matrix_temp[i,j];
        lower_counter <- lower_counter + 1;
 }
 if(i<=j) {
 contact_matrix_temp[i,j] <- contact_matrix_vector[upper_counter];
 upper_counter <- upper_counter + 1;
 }
    }
  }
  upper_simplex_pct <- sum(contact_matrix_vector)/(sum(Lower_Triangular_Simplex)+sum(contact_matrix_vector));
  } //End contact matrix creation.

model:
  {
  real contact_matrix_temp[groups,groups];
  int theta_counter;
  int matrix_counter;
  theta_counter <- 1;
  matrix_counter <- 1;
  for (i in 1:groups) {
for (j in 1:groups) {
        contact_matrix_temp[i,j] <- if_else(i<=j,contact_matrix_vector[matrix_counter],contact_matrix_temp[j,i]*pop_sizes[j]/pop_sizes[i]);
        if (i<=j){
          matrix_counter <- matrix_counter + 1;
        }
theta[y, theta_counter] <- contact_matrix_temp[i,j]*Contact_Matrix_Normalizer;
        theta_counter<-theta_counter+1;
}
}
  }

contact_matrix_vector ~ dirichlet(to_vector(Upper_Contact_Matrix)/(Contact_Matrix_Normalizer*upper_simplex_pct));

Hi David,

I'm with Bob. Not sure I understand you right.
What I get is that you want to constraint a matrix containing counts.
This is what you mentioned with simplex. The simplex construct in 
STAN represents a special vector of probabilities that sum to 1. 

And now as I hope understand right - you have a constraint not
necessarily 1 and its entries are real values. 

For clarity, the following is not highly optimized STAN code
This could be done by STANs softmax function plus
vectorization. 

Lets create a parameter theta which creates a multinomial
'simplex' pr.theta, each 0 <= pr.theta[i] <= 1
and sum(pr.theta) == 1.

sigma.theta ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

theta[1] ~ normal(0, sigma.theta)
theta[2] ~ normal(0, sigma.theta)
theta[3] ~ normal(0, sigma.theta)

pr.theta[1] <- 1/(1+exp(theta[1])+exp(theta[2])+exp(theta[3]))
pr.theta[2] <- exp(theta[1]) * pr.theta[1]
pr.theta[3] <- exp(theta[2]) * pr.theta[1]
pr.theta[4] <- exp(theta[3]) * pr.theta[1]

If you now want to change the upper limit to something else, 
just change
 pr.theta[1] <- 1/(1+exp(theta[1])+exp(theta[2])+exp(theta[3]))
by
 pr.theta[1] <- my_fancy_upper_limit /(1+exp(theta[1])+exp(theta[2])+exp(theta[3]))

Take a look here to:
http://www.mathworks.com/help/stats/multinomial-models-for-nominal-responses.html

Another option you have is to specify a Dirichlet distribution upon a simplex in STAN and 
scale it. 

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/24349692/dirichlet-multinomial-winbugs-code

Andre

parts:
Think of the multinomial distribution — you have a collection of counts
in bins, n_{i}, with the constraint that \sum_{i = 1}^{I} n_{i} = N.  In the
limit of each n_{i} being large, then this can be reasonably approximated
by taking a simplex and scaling each value by N (which was originally
suggested and is equivalent to the softmax construction in the previous
email).  If _any_ of the n_{i} are small, however, then this approximation
falls apart and bad things happen.

Ultimately, however, this is a common mistake of not thinking generatively.
Counts are _data_, and we don’t fit data.  We fit a generative model of
how the data were produced.  So the relevant “contact” matrix isn’t over
counts, it’s over probabilities that could induce said counts.  And those
probabilities can often be easily modeled with simplices.

For example, each column could be a simplex with the corresponding
likelihood a mutlinomial distribution over the counts corresponding to
that column.  Same could be true for the rows.  These are known as
left and right stochastic matrices.

Things become more difficult if you have a double stochastic matrix,
where the rows _and_ columns have to sum to one.  There the matrix
doesn’t decouple into a collection of simplices and you’d have to be
more careful in the implementation (not sure how to do it off the top
of my head).

in bins, n_{i}, with the constraint that \sum_{i = 1}^{I} n_{i} = N.  In the

probabilities can often be easily modeled with simplices.

likelihood a mutlinomial distribution over the counts corresponding to
that column.  Same could be true for the rows.  These are known as
left and right stochastic matrices.

Things become more difficult if you have a double stochastic matrix,
where the rows _and_ columns have to sum to one.  There the matrix
doesn’t decouple into a collection of simplices and you’d have to be
more careful in the implementation (not sure how to do it off the top

Hi Bob,
Sure.

Disease transmission happens when an infected person and a noninfected person come in contact with one another, with some probability p that transmission occurs during that contact. (That probability is a key parameter in infectious disease modeling, which I need to estimate.)

In simple compartmental Epi models, we have a set of groups, or compartments, and we assume that these groups are homogenous. We also assume that the rate at which people contact one another is independent of disease status, so we find the underlying contact rate for different groups. The number of infected individuals in group A at t+1 is the sum over all groups of: ( Percentage of individuals in group i who are sick at time t, multiplied by percentage of individuals in group A that are susceptible at time t, multiplied by the number of contacts between group i and group A per time period, multiplied by the probability p that transmission occurs per contact.)

The contact rate in basic Epi models is frequently assumed or given, but is uncertain. I am attempting to estimate it, based on a prior about what these rates are. The contact rate between each pair of groups is summarized as a matrix - that's what I'm trying to find right now.

2 Constraints exist; 
The matrix is governed by a simple constraint that contacts are symmetric; every contact in group 1 with someone in group 2 is also an contact between the person in group 2 with the person in group 1 - but because the groups are potentially different sizes, the two contact rates are not equal. Instead, you have the reciprical constraint; contact(i,j) = contact(j,i) * size(j)/size(i). 

The matrix also interacts with the probability of transmission, p, since, for example, doubling one and halving the other leaves the outcome the same. In order to control for that, I keep the sum of contacts constant in my model.

I need to model the constraints in order to find a posterior estimate of both the contact matrix and the probability of transmission.

Hope this is clearer,
David Manheim

parts:
Hi Bob,

The model includes both the probability that an uninfected member gets infected, and the rate at which they recover. The reason symmetry is important is that infected people in group 1 infect susceptible people in group 2 at a rate proportional to their contacts - and infected people in group 2 infect susceptible people in group 1 at a rate proportional to the contact. These two processes are constrained, because contact is symmetric. Regarding double counting, this is a continuous diffeq model, so the issue is simplified away; fractional people are infected, and the overlap is incorporated.

Keeping the sum of contacts constant primarily helps with identifiability in the bayesian approximation model. The summary statistic we care about is the R0, the average number of newly infected individuals per infected individual, in a susceptible population - and this is a function of both the contact matrix and the rate.

The data I'm actually modeling isn't included here - but, in part, it is the number of infections observed in each group the subset of patients that show up at clinics that are part of the influenza disease surveillance network. This is an output of the differential equation model, which is based on Michael Betancourt's earlier model (which doesn't contain any subgroups, so it doesn't have these problems.)

Happy to answer any further questions - especially if they help me think about modeling this generatively, instead of my current approach. (But in the mean time, I'm still hoping for a more efficient way to model the contact matrix and its constraints.)

Cheers,
David

parts:
Dear David,

considering the advises from Bob - Markov Chain - and Michael to model counts,
and assuming that your counts are integers you could model them via 
a discrete count distribution (poisson, GPD, negbin) the resulting lambda's 
could form a latent structure corresponding mu's, link: lambda = exp(mu). 

Since you want probabilities for sure, you could get them by la_i / sum(la)
Take a look here:

https://onlinecourses.science.psu.edu/stat504/node/48

Also worth to have a look at the alligator model:
Especially the link between the Poisson and multinomial:

http://www.openbugs.net/Examples/Aligators.html

If your counts are contineous have a look at the gamma distribution.
Andre
